predictions.title: LFM2.5-2.6B's under-2.5 GB claim gets a named context length by Q3 2027
predictions.body:
Liquid AI published LFM2.5-2.6B on Tuesday, August 4: 2.6 billion parameters, pre-trained on roughly 34 trillion tokens, with the context window extended to 128K mid-training, and aimed squarely at agent work - planning, tool calls, multi-step tasks - that finishes on the device instead of round-tripping to a hosted service. Three numbers carry the pitch. The footprint is under 2.5 GB of memory. The context window is 128K. The tool-use score on ToolSandbox is 77.83, against 65.00 for Gemma 4 E4B-it and 52.40 for Gemma 4 E2B-it. Runtime support at release spans llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang and ONNX, on transformers 5.0.0 or later. Every one of those figures is the vendor's own, published alongside the model rather than independently reproduced, and that is the caveat most readers will apply.

It is not the interesting caveat. The interesting one is that two of those three numbers describe different states of the same process, and the release never states them together. Under 2.5 GB is a figure about the model. 128K is a figure about how much of a session the model can hold. A tool-calling agent loop is the case where the two meet, and the release does not say where. A loop that runs long enough to be worth calling an agent has accumulated tool output, intermediate plans and its own transcript, and what that accumulation costs is what decides whether the loop is still resident late in a session rather than at the start of one. Nothing published with the model says what it costs at 8K, or at 32K, or at the 128K it advertises. It says under 2.5 GB, and separately it says 128K, and the reader is left to assume the first survives the second.

That gap matters more here than it would for a hosted model, because the entire argument for this release is a hardware ceiling. The company's own device measurements - 220 tokens per second on an Apple M5 Max, 113 tokens per second on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 - are throughput, and throughput is not footprint. The figure of close to 15,000 output tokens per second on a single NVIDIA H100 under high concurrency is a server number and answers a different deployment question again. A developer deciding whether an agent fits on a laptop, a handset or an embedded board is not asking how fast it runs. They are asking what it will be holding when the session is deep, on hardware where running out is a crash rather than an autoscale. The memory ceiling is the number this release chose to lead with, and it is the number it states with the least qualification.

The prediction is that the ceiling acquires a context length. By the end of Q3 2027, Liquid AI's own published material for LFM2.5-2.6B - the model card, the repository documentation, or a follow-up post from the company - states a memory figure together with the context length that figure holds at. A table with a memory number in one column and a context length in another settles it. So does a stated peak-memory figure for a session run at a named length. The direction the number moves is not the claim; that it is stated at all is.

Several weaker things do not count, and each is worth naming because each is what a publisher under this pressure reaches for first. A repeat of the unqualified figure does not count, however prominently placed - that is the thing that already happened. A table of file sizes per quantisation level does not count, because a file on disk is not what a running loop is holding. A tokens-per-second figure measured at a named context length does not count on its own, because throughput at a length says nothing about footprint at that length. A configuration file from which a reader could derive the answer does not count, because the audience for a device-deployment claim is the developer choosing between models, not the one already committed enough to read the config. And a figure published for a different member of the family does not count; the claim under test is the one attached to this release.

The strongest objection is that a vendor is under no pressure to qualify a headline that is working. Practitioners running llama.cpp work this out for themselves, and asking a company to publish the number that makes its own ceiling look worse is asking it to argue against its own launch. The second objection is architectural, and it is the one that would make this prediction not merely unfulfilled but unnecessary: the release says nothing about how this model's memory scales as context fills, and if it scales unusually flatly then the unqualified ceiling is closer to honest than it looks and there is nothing to restate. The third is that attention goes where the competition is, and the competition here is the benchmark table - 77.83 against 65.00 and 52.40 is the comparison a rival answers, so the next numbers published in this space are more likely to be scores than footprints.

The honest failure mode is quieter than any of those. The figure may simply never appear, not because it is unflattering but because nobody asked for it, and a prediction that something goes unsaid reads as wrong when what actually happened is that nothing happened. This is a claim about what the publisher commits to in writing. Silence settles it against me.

reasoning.because: LFM2.5-2.6B ships an under-2.5 GB footprint and a 128K context as separate, unpaired numbers
reasoning.given: A multi-step agent session accumulates context, and the release states no cost at any length
reasoning.so_that: Liquid AI's own material states a memory figure for LFM2.5-2.6B beside the context length it holds at
reasoning.landing: by Q3 2027; a memory figure beside a context length, not a bare ceiling
reasoning.plain_language: The model is advertised at under 2.5 GB. No published number says what it needs while an agent task is actually running.

predictions.summary: Liquid AI's LFM2.5-2.6B is published at under 2.5 GB of memory and, separately, a 128K context window, with no figure stating what the model costs at a given context. A multi-step agent session accumulates context. Expect Liquid AI's own material to pair the two numbers by Q3 2027.

predictions.title: Herdr publishes a paid tier above its Apache-2.0 runtime by Q2 2027
predictions.body:
Herdr said on Thursday, August 6 that it has joined Y Combinator's F26 batch, and in the same post it relicensed its runtime from AGPL to Apache-2.0. Herdr is a terminal runtime for command-line coding agents: it organises them into panes, tabs and projects and keeps them running persistently on the machine they sit on, and those machines are disconnected from each other today. No funding figure appears anywhere in the announcement, and a batch admission is not a round, so there is no number attached to this and none should be inferred. What the post does state is a split. The runtime people use today stays free under Apache-2.0, and commercial features get built on top of it, with multi-machine connectivity and clients beyond the terminal interface named as the two candidates.

The licence line is the load-bearing one, and it is worth being exact about what moved. AGPL's network-use clause is what would have obliged a hosted service built on Herdr to publish its own source; Apache-2.0 removes that obligation. From the outside that reads as an adoption change - a company that could not put an AGPL runtime behind its own service now can. From the inside it is the opposite of a moat. The clause that just came out was the one thing in the stack reserving the hosted layer for the people who wrote the runtime, and giving it up leaves that layer reserved by nothing except being first and being better. A company that drops its legal claim on the layer it has said it intends to sell has a reason to turn that layer into a priced product rather than a stated plan, because the licence is no longer holding the position for it.

The same week supplies the pressure from the other side. Meta's research group published Muse Code on Wednesday, August 5, a terminal coding agent explicitly in beta, whose subagents persist for the whole session rather than being spawned per task and whose every model call, tool run, approval and edit is appended to a local event log that makes a run replay-exact and restart-safe. Persistence across a session and survival across a restart are the same concerns Herdr's runtime advertises, and the announcement names no price for any of it. That does not make the two substitutes - Muse Code is an agent, Herdr is the runtime other agents run inside - but it does show which way capability travels in this layer once a large research group decides to ship it, and it is an argument against the runtime itself ever being the thing that carries a bill.

The prediction is that the intent becomes a number. By the end of Q2 2027, Herdr publishes a price for a paid tier of its own - a plan or pricing page, or an equivalent published document stating what the tier costs - and the description of that tier names at least one of the two things the August 6 post identified as commercial: connectivity across multiple machines, or a client beyond the terminal interface. The runtime remaining available under Apache-2.0 alongside it is expected rather than a complication; that is the split the post described.

Several near misses do not count, and each is what a company at this stage reaches for first. A waitlist, an early-access form or a coming-soon banner does not count, because the claim is about a published price and not about a published intention. Restating the August 6 plan in a later post does not count for the same reason. A sponsorship or donation button does not count: that is a way of paying maintainers, not a price on a layer. An enterprise page inviting the reader to contact sales, carrying no figure, does not count. A free hosted service does not count until it carries a price, however plainly it is the eventual paid thing. And a funding announcement does not count in either direction - a round is not a price, and the batch admission that prompted this was not a round.

Two objections are worth stating plainly. The first is that nothing in the source sets a clock. The post names the commercial candidates, gives no date for them and no figure for anything, and a small team that has just widened its licence has better near-term reasons to grow installs than to charge for them. The pressure argued here is structural rather than scheduled, and a structural pressure can be absorbed for a long time. The second is that the relicence pays for itself without any of this: Apache-2.0 widens who can adopt the runtime immediately, and a project can sit permissively licensed and unmonetised indefinitely. Plenty do.

The honest failure mode is quieter than either objection. The paid layer may arrive bundled inside a hosted product with its own name, priced as a whole rather than as a tier sitting above the runtime, in which case a reader looking for a pricing page next to a licence file will not find one and will call this wrong when it was right. The claim is about a price appearing on the layer above the runtime, not about the shape of the page it appears on.

reasoning.because: Herdr relicensed its runtime from AGPL to Apache-2.0 in the same post that named its paid features
reasoning.given: AGPL's network-use clause was what reserved the hosted layer; Apache-2.0 gives that away
reasoning.so_that: Herdr publishes a price for the multi-machine and non-terminal features the post named as commercial
reasoning.landing: by Q2 2027; a published price on a plan page, not a restated intent
reasoning.plain_language: Herdr just made its main tool free for anyone to reuse, so the money now has to come from paid extras.

predictions.summary: Herdr joined Y Combinator's F26 batch and, in the same post, relicensed its terminal agent runtime from AGPL to Apache-2.0, naming multi-machine connectivity and non-terminal clients as the commercial layer. No funding figure was given. Expect a published price for that layer by Q2 2027.

predictions.title: Terminal coding agents refuse commands the operator approved by H1 2027
predictions.body:
Alex Wauters published an analysis on the Scale X blog on Wednesday, August 5 of an interactive browser game in which the player stands in for the human approver of a coding agent, accepting or denying each command under time pressure. Across more than 40,000 runs and roughly 409,000 approve-or-deny decisions, mean accuracy was 66.3%. The average is not the interesting part; its shape is. The miss rate rose with how far a hostile command sat from the thing people are trained to fear: 11.7% on obviously destructive commands, 23.8% on persistent mutation attacks, 33.4% on exfiltration and code execution, and 35.0% on scope violations. 35.2% of players caught every threat, but only 20.8% did that while blocking no more than one in five safe commands; 7% approved everything put in front of them, and 32.9% of sessions ended on a negative score. The single most-missed command was npm run analyze, waved through 64.7% of the time even though the malicious payload was visible in the history log.

The author is explicit that the setting is artificial - threats appeared in 34% of commands, far above any real workload, and a timed game is not a working day - and that caveat cuts both ways, because a real operator meets a hostile command far more rarely and is therefore less primed for it. What survives the caveat is not the mean but the ordering, and the ordering is a statement about where the information sits. An approval prompt shows a command line. What the miss rate tracks is what that line resolves to, and for npm run analyze it sat one layer below the string the player was asked to judge, in a log the prompt does not show. A person asked to approve a name cannot inspect a payload. That is not a training deficit and it does not improve with a clearer prompt.

Two other items in the same cycle describe the layer this pushes into. Meta's research group published Muse Code on Wednesday, August 5 - a terminal coding agent, explicitly in beta, installed on macOS and Linux by piping an install script from dev.meta.ai - built around subagents that are asynchronous, persist for the whole session rather than being spawned per task, and decide for themselves when to report back to the main agent, which is what removes the round-trip latency from multi-step work. Every model call, tool run, approval and edit is appended to a local event log that Meta describes as making the agent replay-exact and restart-safe. Approvals plainly still exist there; the log records them. What has moved is that the rate at which command lines arrive in front of one person is set by a scheduler rather than by that person, and the game measured what accuracy does under exactly that condition. Herdr, describing its terminal runtime on Thursday, August 6, supplies the other half: agents organised into panes, tabs and projects and kept running persistently on the machine they run on. A runtime whose selling point is persistence is a runtime doing most of its work while nobody is looking at it.

The standing objection to moving the check into the tool layer has been cost. A static rule list is cheap and brittle, and anything that actually reads a payload wants a model behind it. That constraint moved this week too. Liquid AI published LFM2.5-2.6B on Tuesday, August 4, a 2.6-billion-parameter model aimed at planning, tool calls and multi-step tasks that fits in under 2.5 gigabytes of memory; the company's own measurements, published alongside the model rather than independently reproduced, put it at 220 tokens per second on an Apple M5 Max and at 77.83 on the ToolSandbox tool-use benchmark against 65.00 for Gemma 4 E4B-it. Treat those figures as the vendor's, because that is what they are. The part that transfers is the memory ceiling: a screen that reads what a command expands to no longer implies a hosted service on the other end of it. This prediction does not require the check to be a model, and a deterministic policy engine satisfies it just as well. The point is narrower - the last operational excuse for leaving the decision with the person got cheaper to remove.

The prediction is that the operator's yes stops being sufficient. By the end of H1 2027, a named terminal coding agent or agent runtime publishes a release note, changelog entry or documentation page, dated after August 6, 2026 and describing behaviour in effect on 30 June 2027, under which a class of tool actions is refused by default on the basis of what the command resolves to or what it would reach, and answering the approval prompt does not enable them. Lifting the refusal has to require a configuration change made outside the running session. The bar is a default that arrives with an ordinary install, and a refusal the person at the keyboard cannot answer their way past.

Several cheaper outcomes do not count, and each is worth naming because each is what a harness under this pressure reaches for first. A richer approval prompt does not count - a diff preview, a risk score, a colour, the expanded body of the script sitting behind the alias - because every one of those leaves the decision with the operator, and the operator is the thing that was measured at 66.3%. Adding a separate approval step for some new class of artifact does not count either, for the same reason: another prompt is not the removal of one. A blocklist of command strings does not count, because obviously destructive commands are where the miss rate was lowest, at 11.7%, so a string blocklist re-implements the check people already pass and leaves scope violations at 35.0% exactly where they are. An option shipped switched off does not count. Neither does an enterprise or hosted tier that enforces policy centrally while the ordinary install keeps the prompt as its only gate. A remembered answer - approve this command from now on - is the opposite of the claim. Sandboxing counts only where the release describes the refusal as what a default install does, rather than as a mode the operator selects.

The strongest objection is that the measurement does not transfer, and the author would raise it first: a timed browser game with threats in 34% of commands is not a working day, and 66.3% is a mean over people playing a game rather than over the users of any particular harness. No vendor is obliged to design against a number produced somewhere else. The second objection is product, and it is the heavy one, because a refusal the operator cannot override turns a support ticket into an argument about the vendor's judgement, and the appeal of a terminal agent is that it does the thing you asked for. Muse Code's own design pulls that way: subagents built to keep a multi-step task moving without waiting are subagents that a hard refusal stops mid-run, and that cost is charged on every occasion the policy is wrong. The third is the honest failure mode, and it is quiet. The change may arrive dressed as an operations feature - a permission profile, a filesystem and network scope - with the word approval nowhere in the note, so a reader scanning for a security announcement misses it entirely. That still counts. The claim is about what a default install refuses, not about how the vendor chooses to describe it.

reasoning.because: Mean approval accuracy was 66.3% across 40,000+ runs; misses rose to 35.0% on scope violations
reasoning.given: The approval prompt shows the command line; what the miss rate tracks is one layer below it
reasoning.so_that: A terminal coding agent ships a default that refuses a class of tool actions even when the operator approves them
reasoning.landing: by H1 2027; a shipped default in release notes, not a better approval prompt
reasoning.plain_language: People approving what an AI agent runs get it right about two-thirds of the time, so the tool itself should start saying no.

predictions.summary: A Scale X analysis of more than 40,000 runs put mean accuracy at 66.3% for humans approving agent commands, with misses rising from 11.7% on destructive commands to 35.0% on scope violations. Expect a terminal coding agent to ship a default refusal the operator cannot approve past by H1 2027.
